newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.K. grain at 15-year low as prices slip in Europe.
newsitem.headline: U.K. grain at 15-year low as prices slip in Europe.

text.p: British wheat prices wallowed at their lowest levels for at least 15 years this week, weighed down by a stack of surplus feed wheat and increasingly depressing demand figures just eight weeks away from harvest, grain traders said.
Prices also slipped across much of Europe as the harvest started to reach silos in the south and northern farmers eyed better forecasts for the fast-ripening crop.
The abolition of a controversial European Union wheat export tax eight days ago failed to stop the slide, with exporters concerned over Brussels' silence on when it would open 1997/98 export tenders.

Officials said no decision was expected until at least after the EU farm ministers' meeting next Monday and Tuesday, amid increasing talk that Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler was ready to use export delays as a bargaining chip in EU price talks.

British feed wheat, which missed out on exports as sterling soared and which cannot be put into EU intervention, found few buyers as stocks pressured the market from last year's bumper harvest. Prices eased about 2.50 pounds to 83 pounds for delivered East Anglia harvest wheat for August, traders said.

"I've been in this since 1982 and I can't remember prices as low as this," said one British trader, while the country's Home Grown Cereals Authority talked of prices at their lowest level in two decades -- just one year after prices hit global records.
The stock build-up ends a crop year in which the industry was buffeted by high supplies and the consumer crisis in beef.

One trader said ruminant feed usage in Britain was set to end the July/June campaign at some 3.3 million tonnes, more than a million tonnes below the previous year -- largely because of the consequences of mad cow disease, or BSE.
"BSE has a made a big difference," he said.
On the import side, steadily rising import duties were worsening the pain for millers who bought international wheat at higher prices and now had to import it at higher tariffs.

In France, exporters failed to get much out of the demise of the wheat tax, since the EU replaced the tax with a risky regime of licences which cannot be fixed -- and held back any announcement on the timing of exports at weekly grain talks.
Prices eased over the week but flicked upwards on Friday, especially at southwestern La Pallice, as shippers looked for last-minute supplies to top up the few remaining cargoes.

Wet weather kept downward pressure on prices most of the week as analysts forecast a crop close to last year's record of 34.7 million tonnes. But too much rain could spoil the quality, especially of barley, analysts warned.

Barley was quiet but the year's first new-crop barley deal at Dunkirk, at 845 francs a tonne excluding carrying charges, kept alive speculation that Saudi Arabia, which favours the large port, would soon be back in the world market.
French maize softened in volatile trade despite some demand from Spain -- limited by a new preferential import award of maize from the United States offered by Brussels.
German grain prices drifted in local and export markets.

Brokers said there had been a rush to sell old crop wheat into intervention by the May 31 deadline and this had weighed down prices in June. Germany accounted for more than 80 percent of all EU-controlled grain storage this year.

Additional price pressure came from the fact that traders might withdraw their sales offers of yet undelivered volumes into intervention if they found buyers in the market. This meant the underlying supply situation was comfortable, traders said.
"There is a lot of old crop wheat around at any time, but consumers are well covered ahead of the harvest," one said.
Favourable crop weather also added to the bearish tone, although an early harvest was ruled out because a long period of cold temperatures in the spring slowed crop growth.
Ex-farm sales contracts on the new crop were slow to emerge as buyers and sellers differed by some 15-20 marks a tonne.
Farmgate buyers in eastern Germany were offering 255-260 marks for wheat and 220 marks for barley.
Spain's new harvest has started to arrive, although dealers estimated that less than one quarter has been collected so far.
Feed wheat was available in Andalucia ex-farm at 24,250 pesetas per kg, but in northern Castilla-Leon region prices were higher, at around 25,750 pesetas per kg.
Traders said durum wheat was of variable quality this year, and for that reason quoted price ranges differ widely.
Barley, however, was of good quality.
"We're now getting to reasonable price levels. I don't think prices will get much lower than this," said a Barcelona trader.

Italian soft wheat prices continued falling as demand grew scarce and buyers waited for the new harvest, which the Italian Institute for Agriculture Studies (ISMEA), however, forecasts will be 13.5 percent less than a year ago.
Durum trade was quiet and also concentrating on the new crop. ISMEA forecasts a 4.2 percent drop in the durum wheat harvest due to a 6.2 percent fall in average yields.
